topic: The drone-versus-interceptor cost exchange ratio is the most repeated statistic in air defence, and it is a property of which layer engages — not of the weapons.
researcher: conflict-osint (Dana Okonkwo) via WebSearch/WebFetch — Gauntlet L2 empirical
question: A $4 million interceptor shooting down a $20,000 drone is presented as an unsustainable trade. Is the ratio real, and is it measuring what people think it measures?
verdict: The ratio is arithmetically real and it is the wrong instrument: it is a property of which defensive layer engages, not of the two weapons, and over the same month the same engagement can be computed at 387:1 against the defender or 25:1 for them. The figure that is quoted is the worst cell of a matrix, and the cell is being read as the war.
prior: Written before the first search. I expected the ratio to be real in direction and load-bearing on a contested denominator — that the cheap number excludes the operator, the training and the misses, and that the expensive number is a flyaway procurement figure rather than a replacement cost. I expected attrition and interception tallies to come from belligerents and to be uncheckable. I did not expect to find a published, mainstream counter-literature; I expected to have to construct the opposition.
prior_outcome: discovery, twice over. (1) The counter-case is not merely findable, it is mainstream — CSIS and the Modern War Institute both publish it, which refutes my own L1 expectation and the brief's Phase-1 fallback pressure alike. (2) The load-bearing defect is not the denominator I predicted. It is that the ratio has no fixed value at all: the layer that engages moves it by roughly four orders of magnitude, and the quoted figure is a selection, not a measurement. My prior about belligerent counting was a mirror and is confirmed unchanged.
domains: the-price — unit costs on both sides, and the spread inside each
the-baseline — where this ratio sits in the historical distribution of air-defence cost exchange (MANDATORY row)
the-engagement — which layer actually engages what, and the plumbing of the kill chain
the-count — who counts an interception, by what method, and who checks
industrial-base — production rates and magazine depth on both sides
procurement-politics — budget lines authorised versus delivered
the-counter-case — the strongest published argument that the ratio is the wrong metric (MANDATORY row)

tension.expectation: A cheap attack drone against an expensive interceptor is a new and unsustainable cost exchange — the defender is being bankrupted one shot at a time, and this is a distinctive feature of the drone era.
tension.reality: The ratio has no single value. Computed from published unit costs over the same month of the same war, it runs from 387:1 against the defender (a PAC-3 MSE against a low-end Shahed estimate) to about 25:1 in the defender's favour (a $2,000 interceptor drone against a $50,000 Shahed) — a span of roughly 9,700x, driven entirely by which layer engages. And the adverse end sits inside a distribution that has been running since 2011: Iron Dome's own recomputable band is 62.5:1 to 266.7:1.
tension.why_it_is_a_tension: Shape 5 — the category error. The subject is being measured with an instrument that returns a different answer depending on an input nobody quotes. It is not that the famous number is false; it is that it is one cell of a matrix being read as a scalar, and the baseline row shows the adverse cell is not new. DOWNGRADED from high to moderate per Phase 2: the counter-case at `sm-value-not-cost` survives Phase 6 — CSIS's and the Modern War Institute's argument that the correct comparison is the interceptor against the LOSS PREVENTED, not against the threat destroyed, stands unrefuted and is not answered by anything I found. It does not win, because it does not dissolve the magazine-depth problem, but it survives, so the strength comes down one step.
tension.strength: moderate — the premise is checkable and widely held; it is not demonstrably wrong, it is under-determined, and a surviving counter-case took it down one step
tension.strength_note: FIELD CONFLICT, recorded rather than resolved. `pipeline/NOTEBOOK-SCHEMA.md:55` still defines high as 'checkable, widely held, and demonstrably wrong' — three conjoined properties. `pipeline/RESEARCH-PROMPT.md:79` now says strength 'stays a judgement about how checkable the tension is, not how large it is'. Those are two different fields with one name. I graded against the prompt, because it is the later document, and I am saying so rather than picking silently.

normal_range: Air-defence cost exchange has run heavily adverse for the entire modern era of the metric. Iron Dome, in continuous operation since 2011, is quoted at 100:1–500:1 adverse; its own published component prices recompute to 62.5:1–266.7:1 (see f-irondome-recompute). The PAC-3-versus-Shahed band of 20:1–387:1 overlaps that distribution across most of its range. This instance is NOT outside normal variation for the adverse cell. What is outside normal variation is the FAVOURABLE cell — a defender fielding a $2,000 interceptor against a $10,000–$50,000 threat is the new observation, and it is the one that is not being quoted.

facts.claim: The quoted 100:1–500:1 Iron Dome range is not recomputable from the component prices quoted beside it: those prices yield 62.5:1 to 266.7:1, and no pair inside the stated bands reaches 500:1
facts.method: Cheapest interceptor over dearest rocket: 50,000/800 = 62.5. Dearest interceptor over cheapest rocket: 80,000/300 = 266.67. The stated lower bound of 100:1 IS reachable (50,000/500 = 100, and $500 is inside the $300–$800 band). The stated upper bound of 500:1 is NOT reachable from any pair in the stated bands; it would require a rocket priced at $160 against the dearest interceptor. Either the headline range is drawn from figures other than the ones printed beside it, or it is wrong.

mechanisms.name: The ratio is a property of the layer, not of the weapons
chain: A published cost-exchange ratio picks one defensive round and one threat airframe and divides
BUT a layered air defence fields several rounds at once, spanning three orders of magnitude in price, and assigns them by what the radar track looks like in the seconds available
THEREFORE the ratio realised on any given night is a weighted average over the assignment, not the price of the dearest round
BUT the assignment is decided under time pressure on an unlabelled track — speed, altitude, heading and radar cross-section, with asymmetric cost of error
THEREFORE the defender will sometimes spend a strategic interceptor on a cheap drone, and the famous ratio is the price of that specific mistake rather than the price of the campaign

steps.text: A published cost-exchange ratio picks one defensive round and one threat airframe and divides
A layered air defence fields several rounds simultaneously, spanning three orders of magnitude in price
The ratio realised on a given night is a weighted average over the assignment, not the price of the dearest round
The assignment is decided in seconds on an unlabelled radar track with asymmetric cost of error
The famous ratio is the price of a specific assignment error, not the price of the campaign

mechanisms.explains: Why the same engagement computes to 387:1 against and 25:1 for, and why both numbers are honestly derived

mechanisms.name: How a 92% interception rate is manufactured, without anyone lying
chain: A belligerent publishes a nightly count of launches and of targets shot down or suppressed
BUT the shot-down category combines kinetic kills with electronic-warfare neutralisations, and the reporting window covers roughly 14 of every 24 hours
THEREFORE the published rate is a ratio between two numbers supplied by the same interested party, over a partial window, on a category that does not mean what the word means
BUT a research institute compiles the series and publishes a monthly analysis, disclosing its sourcing plainly
THEREFORE the number acquires a second citation without acquiring a second observation, and downstream it reads as corroborated

steps.text: A belligerent publishes a nightly count of launches and of targets shot down or suppressed
The shot-down category merges kinetic kills with EW neutralisations, and the window covers roughly 14 of 24 hours
The published rate is one interested party's numerator over its own denominator, on a partial window, on a merged category
A research institute compiles the series into a monthly analysis and discloses its sourcing plainly
The number gains a second citation without gaining a second observation, and reads downstream as corroborated

mechanisms.explains: Why no cost-per-intercept can be computed for this campaign at all, and why the number that looks best-sourced is the one with the fewest observations behind it
mechanisms.note: Nobody in this chain does anything wrong. The Air Force reports what it counts, the institute discloses its method, the press cites the institute. The defect is emergent and that is why it is a mechanism rather than an accusation.

reversals.obvious_reading: A four-million-dollar missile shooting down a twenty-thousand-dollar drone is an obviously losing trade, and you do not need a defence economist to see it. The attacker buys a hundred of something for the price of one of yours. Run that for a year and the magazine is empty and the budget is gone. This is the clearest thing in modern war and everyone from procurement officials to the people quoting it on television has the arithmetic right.
reversals.why_wrong: The arithmetic is right and the selection is not. That engagement happened; it is one cell of a matrix. Over the same month, in the same campaign, the same threat was also being engaged by a two-thousand-dollar airframe — and by that pairing the defender is twenty-five to one ahead. Both numbers come from published prices. Neither is a lie. The ratio has no value until you say which layer, and nobody who quotes it says which layer.
reversals.escalation: And the span between the best and worst cell is roughly nine thousand seven hundred times. A metric whose plausible range covers four orders of magnitude on an input nobody states is not measuring the war.

reversals.obvious_reading: Whatever the exact figure, the direction is new. Cheap mass-produced attack drones have inverted an economics that used to favour the defender, and that inversion is the defining change of this decade of warfare.
reversals.why_wrong: The adverse cell is not new. Iron Dome has run at a heavily adverse cost exchange since 2011 — the recomputable band from its own published component prices is 62.5:1 to 266.7:1 — and the PAC-3-against-Shahed band overlaps that across most of its range. Air defence has always cost more per round than what it shoots at; that is what the round is for. The genuinely new observation is the other cell, the one nobody quotes: a defender fielding a two-thousand-dollar interceptor against a twenty-thousand-dollar threat is the first favourable cost exchange in the modern history of the metric, and it is being reported as a footnote to a crisis.
reversals.escalation: The story that got told is the expensive half of a change whose cheap half is the actual news.

reversals.obvious_reading: Set the money aside — the defence is working. Ninety-two per cent of incoming drones are being stopped, and that figure is compiled and published by an independent research institute, not by a government press office.
reversals.why_wrong: The institute says, in its own methodology, that the figure comes exclusively from one belligerent's daily reports. The category counted is 'shot down or suppressed', which merges a drone destroyed by an interceptor with a drone jammed into the ground. The reporting window covers roughly fourteen of every twenty-four hours. And no independent body validates the aggregate for either side. The ninety-two per cent is arithmetically correct — five thousand two hundred and eighty-five over five thousand seven hundred and forty-nine — and it is a number one interested party computed from its own count of both halves.
reversals.escalation: Fifty-one years after the last engagement of the Vietnam air war, with both archives open, the two sides' figures for the same missiles still differ by up to an order of magnitude. That is how long a belligerent attrition claim takes to settle, and this one is two months old.

steel_man.claim: The cost-exchange ratio is the wrong comparison, but the people quoting it are directionally right and the correction does not rescue the defender.
steel_man.statement: You are correcting a comparison that was never meant to be precise, and the correction cuts against you. The relevant number is not the interceptor against the threat; it is the interceptor against the loss prevented — the substation, the barracks, the city block. On that comparison a four-million-dollar round is cheap and the whole cost-exchange frame is a category error in the other direction. Air defence is a reliability problem under zero tolerance for failure: you cannot decline the expensive engagement because the track was ambiguous and you had nine seconds. And the cheap-interceptor layer does not dissolve the problem. It is real, it is impressive, and it is a layer — it does not engage ballistic threats, it does not engage cruise missiles, and the sensor chain that makes a two-thousand-dollar airframe lethal is not two thousand dollars. Ukraine did not stop buying Patriot rounds. One can win every engagement on the favourable exchange and still lose, because magazine depth, not unit price, is the binding constraint, and no defence budget in the world is structured to sustain the adverse cell indefinitely.
steel_man.why_include: Because it is right about the frame and I am not going to win by pretending otherwise, and because the video's own verdict — the ratio measures the layer, not the war — is answered by it: yes, and the layer you cannot avoid is the expensive one. It survives. It does not win, because it does not explain why the metric's own range spans four orders of magnitude or why the favourable cell went unreported. Per Phase 2 it takes `tension.strength` down one step, and I have applied that.
steel_man.provenance_note: SCHEMA DEFECT, recorded. `steel_man.provenance` is mandated twice by `pipeline/RESEARCH-PROMPT.md` (lines 51 and 125) and by the quality bar's 'if constructed, it says so' row — and it is declared NOWHERE: not in `NOTEBOOK-SCHEMA.md`'s `steel_man` field list (line 137), not in the consumer table, and not in `SteelMan` in `app/_phases/_shared/notebook/types.ts:197-202`. I have written it anyway because the prompt names it. Under the schema's own Rule 11 it should not ship.

counter_positions_to_state_fairly.position: The interception rates published by both belligerents should be treated as operational reporting rather than as propaganda, because a force that systematically inflates its own air-defence performance degrades its own targeting and resource allocation — the internal audience for these numbers is real.
counter_positions_to_state_fairly.holder: defence analysts who work with open-source military reporting
counter_positions_to_state_fairly.locator: argued in general terms across the defence-analysis commentary surveyed; not attributed to a named individual in this notebook by choice

counter_positions_to_state_fairly.position: The unit prices quoted for cheap interceptors are procurement-advocacy figures and should be discounted accordingly — the party quoting them is seeking allied funding for the programme in the same period.
counter_positions_to_state_fairly.holder: this notebook, against its own most attractive fact
counter_positions_to_state_fairly.locator: f-ratio-interceptor is graded `low` and flagged on exactly this ground

scale_conversions.raw: The cost exchange ratio spans 387:1 against to 25:1 for, a factor of roughly 9,700
scale_conversions.felt: It is the difference between a metric that says you are losing badly and the same metric, the same month, the same war, saying you are winning comfortably — and the only thing that changed is which of your own weapons fired.
Nineteen times, for one object. Before anyone has picked a defender's round, the attacker's price tag alone can move the famous ratio by a factor of nineteen.

scale_conversions.raw: $3.871 million per PAC-3 MSE, FY2026 flyaway
scale_conversions.felt: $3.871 million, per the Army's FY2026 procurement justification. Quoted exactly and with its vintage, because a filed figure's precision is the handle you have on it — and because I have not read the exhibit line myself, only two reports of it.

scale_conversions.raw: 5,285 of 5,749 reported shot down or suppressed, June 2026 — 91.93%
scale_conversions.felt: Ninety-two per cent, computed by one side from its own count of both the shots and the hits, over about fourteen hours of each day, on a category that counts a jammed drone and a destroyed one as the same event.

analogy_candidates.analogy: Quoting the cost-exchange ratio without naming the layer is like quoting a hospital's cost per patient using only the intensive-care ward. The number is real, the ward is real, and it is not the hospital.

A company reporting its own revenue, its own costs and its own margin, with no auditor — and a respected journal publishing a quarterly analysis of the figures the company reported. The journal is honest, its methodology page says so, and by the third citation the number has become 'independently analysed'.

candidate_questions: What is the cost exchange ratio actually a ratio of?
Who counts an interception, and does anyone check?
If the cheap layer is doing most of the work, why is the expensive number the one that circulates?
Is an adverse air-defence cost exchange new, or is it what air defence has always looked like?

unknowns.why: Nobody publishes it. The single-shot probability of kill for a $2,000 airframe is the input that decides whether the favourable ratio is 25:1 or 3:1 or worse, and it is the one number neither the manufacturers nor the ministry states.
unknowns.impact: The script may state the DIRECTION of the interceptor-drone exchange — that it is favourable to the defender — and may never state a favourable ratio as a figure. No '25 to 1'.

unknowns.what: The cost of the detection, cueing and control chain that a cheap interceptor depends on
unknowns.why: Every quoted interceptor price is an airframe price. The radar, the acoustic sensor network and the fire-control that put the airframe on the target are excluded and unpriced in everything I found.
unknowns.impact: The script must not present the cheap-interceptor figure as a system cost. Say 'the airframe costs', never 'it costs'.

unknowns.what: What share of 'shot down or suppressed' is kinetic destruction and what share is electronic-warfare neutralisation
unknowns.why: The categories are merged at source and neither belligerent separates them.
unknowns.impact: The script may never compute or state a cost per intercept for this campaign. Not as a figure, not as an approximation, not as a range.

unknowns.why: The document is published and its host returned 403 to this run on 2026-08-12.
unknowns.impact: The script attributes the figure as 'reported from the Army's FY2026 justification', never as 'the Army's budget says'. The distinction is one word and it is the whole of my discipline.

unknowns.why: A hit is not a kill, and the two accounts use different words. The 3x–15x disagreement may be partly definitional.
unknowns.impact: The script says the two sides' accounts 'still differ' and never quantifies the disagreement. No 'by a factor of fifteen'.

unknowns.why: It is not reachable from any pair of component prices printed alongside it.

obligations.must: Whenever a cost-exchange ratio is spoken, name the layer it was computed on in the same sentence.
obligations.why: The entire thesis is that the ratio is meaningless without it. A render that states the ratio and names the layer in the next beat has already made the error the video is about.

obligations.must: State that the interceptor-drone exchange is favourable to the defender, and state that the magnitude is not publicly derivable and why.
obligations.why: u-interceptor-pk removes the figure. Without a matching must-say the render will simply route around the finding, and the favourable cell going unreported is half the video's point — a script that also fails to report it has enacted its own subject.

obligations.must: Every interception figure spoken in the script is attributed in the same sentence to the party that produced it — 'the Ukrainian Air Force reported', 'the Russian defence ministry reported' — and the script states once, explicitly, that no independent body validates either.
obligations.why: This is the single requirement of my beat. `kind: utterance` records it in the notebook; nothing carries it to the render, so it is written here as a must-say the render gate can fail on.

obligations.must: If one belligerent's interception claim is stated, the other's is stated in the same segment and held to the same standard.
obligations.why: A script that treats one side's unverifiable claim as data and the other's as propaganda has made a choice the evidence does not support. The symmetry is the discipline.

obligations.must: State plainly, once, that no independent body counts interceptions for this campaign and that this is a finding rather than a caveat.
obligations.why: f-no-independent-verification is `kind: absence`, load-bearing, and the most important thing in the notebook. A hedge is not a delivery of it.

engine_fit.why: Four candidate readings genuinely compete: the ratio is real and decisive / real but describing a minority of engagements / a measurement artefact of layer selection / the right number for the wrong question. The D-honest tell — 'is the premise itself in the candidate set?' — is satisfied, because the premise (the ratio measures the war) is candidate one and must be adjudicated first.
engine_fit.hazard: Adjudication renders as a ruling. On a subject where the underlying counts are two months old, unverified and supplied by interested parties, a confident ruling is a stronger claim than the evidence can carry — and the engine's pleasure is the confidence of the verdict. Mitigable: the ruling must be about the METRIC, which is fully checkable, and never about the campaign, which is not.

engine_fit.why: Three genuine reversals are pre-computed and they escalate cleanly: the ratio is a selection, the adverse cell is not new, the rate is one party's own arithmetic.
engine_fit.hazard: The chain's load-bearing move is the self-attack, which requires having proved something first. This notebook never reaches proof — it reaches 'the metric is under-determined' — so the reversal has to turn on a claim it only weakened. Rendered anyway, the engine supplies a certainty the material does not have.

engine_fit.why: Structurally an excellent fit: the kill chain is a mechanism a viewer could operate, and the engine's pleasure is disproportion between labour and reward.
engine_fit.hazard: HIGH FIT, HIGH HAZARD, and this is the cell the axis exists for. The disproportion between labour and reward IS the meme this notebook refutes. Engine B renders this material as the exact video it disputes, and renders it well. This is not a poor fit and grading it poor would hide the engine from the person selecting it. Do not select.

engine_fit.hazard: Low. The briefing form's dating discipline is protective here rather than risky.

Needs naturally ordered difficulty. The material is a matrix, not a ladder.
engine_fit.hazard: If forced, the rungs would become escalating classes of target — substation, barracks, city block. Per ENGINES.md the ladder is hazardous where the rungs are people, and the top rung here is the thing you cannot be funny about.

engine_fit.hazard: A withholding fifty-second clip about contested attrition figures in an active war is a thing that gets stripped of context and reposted. The withholding is the hazard, not a side effect of it. Do not select.

currency.half_life: About four months for the quantities; roughly two years for the argument.
currency.why: Interceptor unit prices are falling fast and the layer mix is moving month to month. The structural claim — that a cost-exchange ratio is a property of the layer and that nobody who quotes it names the layer — outlives every figure in the notebook.
currency.advice: Speak the interceptor exchange as a direction, never a level — 'the cheap layer is ahead' survives a year, '25 to 1' is wrong next quarter. Speak the PAC-3 figure exactly and with its vintage, because it is a filed number and rounding it destroys the reader's only handle. And date every interception claim in the sentence that carries it: 'in June, the Air Force reported' ages honestly in a way that 'ninety-two per cent are stopped' does not.

research_gaps: THE PRIMARY SOURCE I NAMED AND DID NOT READ. The Army FY2026 Missile Procurement justification book is published at asafm.army.mil and returned HTTP 403 to this run's fetch tool on 2026-08-12. f-pac3-unit is load-bearing and quantitative and therefore fails the schema's Rule 4 unless this gap is named. It is named. The figure is carried at `medium` on two agreeing secondary reports, and the exhibit line, the quantity and the cost basis are unread.

No Ukrainian- or Russian-language sources were searched. Both belligerents' primary reporting is in those languages and this run read only English restatements of it — including the daily channel that is the origin of every interception figure in this notebook.

The Ukrainian Air Force daily channels (t.me/kpszsu, facebook.com/kpszsu) were not read directly. Every interception figure here is at second or third hand from the party that published it, which is the exact laundering path f-isis-derives-from-belligerent describes. I am inside my own finding.

No visually-confirmed loss database (Oryx-class) was consulted, because interceptions have no visual-confirmation equivalent — you cannot geolocate a drone that did not arrive. This is a permanent structural gap in the domain, not an omission by this run, but it means the class of evidence my discipline is built on is entirely absent from this notebook.

Iron Dome costings were taken from aggregators. No primary Israeli procurement document was reached, which is why f-irondome-recompute can show the published range is unreproducible but cannot say which of the two figures is right.

The CSIS and MWI counter-case articles were read via search summary, not fetched in full. The steel-man is FOUND and its shape is confirmed, but I have not read either argument at length and may be understating it.

Magazine depth and production rates on both sides were not searched at all — an entire declared domain (industrial-base) went unworked. The steel-man rests part of its weight there and I did not go and check.

Not chased: whether any insurance, municipal or utility damage-record series exists that would permit an independent impact count, which is the most likely route to ending f-no-independent-verification.
